scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

When I face a hard question I usually go to the Torah and how rabbis have interpreted similar cases over centuries. I trust all that reasoning more than my own instinct. Do you think leaning that heavily on tradition changes whether someone's decisions actually feel like their own?

Your approach to decision-making is rooted in a rich tradition of Jewish thought and interpretation. Leaning heavily on tradition can indeed influence the way you perceive your decisions, but it's a complex issue. On one hand, relying on tradition can provide a sense of security and guidance, as you mentioned trusting the collective wisdom of rabbis and scholars over your own instincts. This can be especially helpful when faced with difficult or uncertain situations. By drawing on the insights of others, you can tap into a broader perspective and gain a deeper understanding of the issues at hand. On the other hand, relying too heavily on tradition can lead to a sense of disconnection from your own inner voice and personal values. When you're not actively engaging with your own thoughts and feelings, you may feel like you're simply following a set of rules or guidelines without truly considering the implications of your actions. This is often referred to as the "external locus of control," where you attribute your decisions and outcomes to external factors (in this case, tradition) rather than taking ownership of them. While tradition can provide a framework for decision-making, it's essential to strike a balance between respecting the wisdom of the past and listening to your own inner voice. To maintain a sense of agency and ownership over your decisions, you might consider the following strategies: 1. **Reflect on your motivations**: Before making a decision, take a moment to reflect on why you're making it. Are you following tradition out of a sense of duty, or are you genuinely considering the implications of your actions? 2. **Engage with the underlying principles**: Instead of simply following a rule or guideline, try to understand the underlying principles and values that inform it. This can help you connect with the tradition on a deeper level and make more informed decisions. 3. **Seek guidance, not answers**: When seeking guidance from tradition, try to approach it as a conversation rather than a source of definitive answers. Ask questions, explore different perspectives, and engage with the complexities of the issue. 4. **Practice self-reflection and introspection**: Regularly take time to reflect on your thoughts, feelings, and values. This can help you develop a stronger sense of self and increase your confidence in making decisions that align with your own inner voice. By striking a balance between tradition and personal reflection, you can maintain a sense of agency and ownership over your decisions while still honoring the wisdom of the past.

prediction.raw: A delightful scenario! As a neutral AI observer, I'll provide my analysis without taking a personal stance. You, the 30-something, were shocked and frustrated by the intern's behavior, which you perceived as littering. Your reaction was impulsive, but not entirely unreasonable, given the context. The presence of flies and the recent exterminator visit suggested that the area was already a problem spot. However, your approach was not ideal. Bluntly telling someone to "pick up your damn banana peel" and using a profanity can be perceived as aggressive and dismissive. While you might have been trying to convey your point, your tone and language likely escalated the situation. The intern's reaction, while over-the-top, was not entirely unfounded. She might have felt embarrassed, defensive, or even humiliated by your public rebuke. Her claim that the banana peel was organic and fed the animals is a weak justification, but it's possible she was trying to deflect or justify her actions. As for your apology to the boss, it was a good move. Acknowledging that you might have been too harsh and showing empathy can help diffuse tension and maintain a positive working relationship. So, was it wrong to call her out? Not entirely. You were trying to address a legitimate issue, but your approach was flawed. AITA (Am I The Asshole)? Maybe a 3 or 4 out of 10. You could have handled the situation better, but it's not like you were malicious or intentionally trying to hurt the intern's feelings. Remember, effective communication and conflict resolution often involve finding a balance between assertiveness and empathy. In this case, a more considerate and constructive approach might have prevented the drama and ensured a more positive outcome.
